Another mode of travel appropriate for seniors is slow travel.
Slow travel consists of going to a single location where you stay at a B&B, hotel/mo-tel, vacation home, or apartment for an extended stay.
You can then leisurely explore, get to know the culture, and relax.
Grand Tours are excellent for seniors because they handle all aspects of the trip, such as trans-portation, meals, activities, and sightseeing desti-nations.
Plus, you have the advantage of making friends because you will be together for the whole trip.
If this type of travel appeals to you, the Four Seasons Travel Club runs several of them a year, where you can join members of our community for an exciting adventure.

However, there are some caveats for seniors, which you can read about in Frank Mongiello’s article in this issue.
The types of travel we have described have a host of advantages, but only if you ensure your safety as well.
The National Council on Aging recommends that you check with your doctor before you go and follow public health guidelines for the places you visit.

While traveling on a bus or plane, make sure you keep hydrated, don’t sit too long in one position, pack antibacterial wipes, and always keep your medicines and documents with you, especially your credit cards ( ncoa.org ).
If you keep these tips in mind, you should be able to have an exciting and meaningful adventure traveling in keeping with your physical condition and overall health.

Should I take a cruise?
Is it a good way to travel?
Is it safe?
Is it worth the price?
What is a river cruise like?
These are some questions that travel agents frequently receive.
Cruising is popular.
Recent statistics show that cruising is on the rise, and river cruising (both in the U.S. and abroad) is in demand.
The cruise industry has experienced record sales since the pandemic.
This year, cruising surpassed the pre-pandemic numbers by a large margin.

Always purchase travel insurance; you just never know.
Unforeseen circumstances can happen, pre-cruise, or even during the cruise.
Some people believe that if you become ill or if a tragic event occurs, the cruise lines will refund your money.
This is not true.
The cruise lines like to have fully-booked ships.
It’s purely a busi-ness decision.
The cruise lines will lose money if a room is unoccupied.
Again, always purchase travel insurance; it protects your investment in case something goes wrong.
When passengers become ill on board, they may need to be airlifted by helicopter to the near-est port.
It can cost over $150,000 to airlift one person.
Without insurance, you will be responsible for this amount.
Unfortunately, as we age, the cost of travel insurance increases, but it is well worth spending a few hundred dollars instead of losing thousands.
Medicare and many secondary insurance companies are not accepted overseas.
Some people believe that their credit card company automatically provides travel insurance.
Some do, but they pay out a minimal amount.

Each cruise line offers various levels of state -rooms, from an interior cabin (sort of like a large walk-in closet), ocean view rooms with a porthole or square window (which will not open for obvious reasons), balconies, mini suites, or larger suites.
The price can increase for each room type, but sometimes you can get a deal where a balcony room is priced lower than an ocean view.
Always do your research.

Many of the ocean view rooms are located on the lower level of the ship, so if you’re concerned about becoming seasick, book on a lower deck.
Another great location is an aft-facing room (at the rear of the ship).
This is where you will enjoy a wonderful panoramic view of the ocean, and will enjoy a smoother sailing.
The main dining rooms are always located at the rear of the ship on a lower deck(s) for this reason.
These rooms can be a bit pricy.
You can book an assigned cabin or a “guaran-tee” cabin that is lower in price.
This means you select your room type, but not its exact location.
The cruise line will assign a room to you before your embarkation date.
If you’re a gambler, you may want to save by booking a “guarantee room,” that could put you anywhere on the ship.
You can book a room on a future cruise at the Future Cruise Desk of your current cruise.
The advantage of booking a cruise in advance is that you get the best rate available (although, as mentioned earlier, the price you paid can drop).
The cruise lines may offer a reduced deposit.
